\chapter{Day}
\label{ch:ta-day}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use \ta{நாள்} as the everyday word for day and keep \ta{தினம்} for the formal compounds where it actually belongs.}

Say mūnṟu nāḷ for three days and sutantira tiṉam for Independence Day, classifying each as everyday-native or formal-Sanskrit.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ta{நாள்}]{\ta{நாள்} (nāḷ) — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} the one this arc's Dravidian languages didn't lose}

\label{lesson:TA-C23-naal}



\begin{quote}
You've now seen three Dravidian languages reach for a loanword — Sanskrit, twice, and Persian once — to name their everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{} Tamil doesn't. This lesson is about the one that didn't.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{நாள்}} (\textbf{nāḷ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} — is native \textbf{Dravidian}, from \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*nāḷ}}. You've already met it, hiding inside \textbf{\ta{நாளை}} (\emph{nāḷai}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 4). But here's the honest headline of this lesson: \ta{நாள்} isn't a survivor clinging to one narrow sense the way some native Dravidian words are — it is simply Tamil's \textbf{plain, everyday, unmarked} word for counting a day, as ordinary as \textbf{\ta{மூன்று} \ta{நாள்}} (\emph{mūnṟu nāḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{three days}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}

  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāḷ\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} native Dravidian, already met inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mūnṟu nāḷ\textquotedblright{} — three days
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did you already meet \textbf{\ta{நாள்}} before this lesson? (Inside \textbf{\ta{நாளை}}, \emph{nāḷai}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 4.) Is Tamil's everyday day-word a loanword? (\textbf{No} — \textbf{\ta{நாள்}} is native Dravidian.) Is it marginal or literary? (\textbf{No} — it is the plain everyday counting word.) Next: compare the other sisters' borrowed day-words and Tamil's formal \emph{tiṉam}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ta{நாள்} / \ta{தினம்}]{\ta{நாள்} and \ta{தினம்} — everyday native, formal borrowed}

\label{lesson:TA-C23-day-family-register}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Nāḷ} is plainly native and everyday. Put that lexical choice beside the other Dravidian tracks.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Four everyday day-words}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Kannada \textbf{dina} — Sanskrit tatsama
  \item Telugu \textbf{rōju} — Persian loan
  \item Malayalam \textbf{divasam} — Sanskrit tatsama
  \item Tamil \textbf{nāḷ} — native Dravidian
\end{itemize}

Tamil is the only one here whose unmarked everyday counting word remains native.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Tamil still has \ta{தினம்}}
\textbf{\ta{தினம்}} (\emph{tiṉam}) is the same Sanskrit \emph{dina} as Kannada/Malayalam, ultimately from PIE \emph{\textbf{dyew-}}, \textquotedblleft{}shine,\textquotedblright{} also behind Latin \emph{diēs}. Tamil assigns it formal and compound work: \textbf{\ta{சுதந்திர} \ta{தினம்}}, \textquotedblleft{}Independence Day,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ta{தினசரி}}, \textquotedblleft{}daily.\textquotedblright{} Casual counting remains \emph{nāḷ}.

The language did not reject the loan; it gave native and borrowed forms different jobs.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}mūnṟu nāḷ\textquotedblright{} — three days
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}sutantira tiṉam\textquotedblright{} — Independence Day
  \item \emph{Sort:} everyday native · formal/compound Sanskrit
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which track alone keeps a native everyday day-word? (\textbf{Tamil}.) Where does \emph{tiṉam} appear? (\textbf{Formal compounds}.) Is it unrelated to Kannada \emph{dina}? (\textbf{No} — it is the same Sanskrit tatsama.)
\end{tcolorbox}
